facts.name: Showy Goldenrod
facts.moisture: Dry to average; drought tolerant once settled
facts.notes: A well-behaved Michigan native goldenrod: upright wands of gold that bloom a little later than most goldenrods, a late nectar source for monarchs and other pollinators. Unlike Canada goldenrod, it isn't known to be weedy, and it handles dry sites.

credit.by: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service - Midwest Region

sources.title: MSU Native Plants: Showy goldenrod
sources.note: Michigan native perennial in MSU's native plant trials; late bloomer that suits dry sites, and unlike Canada goldenrod it isn't known to be a weed.

sources.title: Wild Ones Keweenaw (Michigan): Showy Goldenrod
sources.note: Michigan native plant sheet: blooms later than most goldenrods, a late nectar source for monarchs and other pollinators.

sources.title: MSU Native Plants: Showy goldenrod fact sheet (PDF)
sources.note: Native east of the Rocky Mountains; tested at MSU for plants blooming mid-August through early October.

sources.title: Delaware Nature (DNRT): Showy Goldenrod
sources.note: 1 to 3 ft; open woods and prairies; blooms August to September.

companions.why: Pair with fall aster, bugbane, eupatorium, goldenrod, sedum or toad lily; near bleeding heart; with variegated hosta and grasses.

sources.title: Wisconsin Horticulture (UW–Madison Extension): Japanese Anemone article

companions.why: Combines with yellow flowers such as coreopsis and goldenrod, pink ones such as purple coneflower, prairie grasses and silver plants such as Stachys (lamb's ear).

sources.title: Wisconsin Horticulture (UW–Madison Extension): Blazing Star article

companions.why: A border is brightened when obedient plant is planted alongside goldenrods, little bluestem and purple coneflower.
